SUTR-9 — SuperUnicode Mathematical Notation and Layout Support (SUMNLS)

The mathematical character repertoire, the math property set, and the kernel box-model layout engine across the SUCS and ExtSUCS codepoint space

Standard ID: SUTR-9
Status: 0.1.0 — Published
Scope: The mathematical character repertoire, the math property set, and the kernel box-model layout engine across the SUCS and ExtSUCS codepoint space
Applies to: SUCD, SUTR-0 (SUCS Core), SUTR-6 (Bridge), SUTR-7 (SUCEM), SUTR-8 (SUCPM), SUAS-002 (SGW), SUAS-003 (SBR), SUAS-005 (SSP), the SUF vector font engine, and every math-consuming layout subsystem
Last updated: 2026-10-18
Source: docs/sutr/SUTR-9-sumnls.md — this page is generated from it, and the repository copy governs where they differ.

1. Overview

Where UTR #25 Unicode Support for Mathematics describes how mathematics is represented in the Unicode repertoire and laid out in OpenType MATH fonts, SUTR-9 (SUMNLS) establishes the equivalent contract for SuperUnicode: the character repertoire, the O(1) property flags, the zero-allocation spatial layout engine, and the in-band System Control Plane directives that together let a freestanding SuperUnicode kernel render mathematical notation without a markup-aware font stack and without a heap.

The report answers four questions that every math consumer must share:

  1. Which characters make up the mathematical repertoire, and how are the alphabetic style variants encoded?
  2. What properties does a math consumer read to classify an operator, and how are they evaluated in O(1)?
  3. How is a formula laid out into stacked fractions, radicals, extensible delimiters, and script tiers with a single, allocation-free pass?
  4. How is math context carried in-band so a plain 64-bit code unit stream is self-describing to the layout engine?

The first two are the subject of the UTR #25-style body (§2–§4). The third and fourth are the SuperUnicode-specific architecture of §5 and §6.

1.1 Relation to UTR #25

SUMNLS is the SuperUnicode analog of UTR #25 Unicode Support for Mathematics. It adopts that report's framing: the mathematical repertoire, the Math property, the MathClass classification of operators, the mathematical alphanumeric symbol styles, and the OpenType MATH model of fractions, radicals, scripts, and extensible delimiters. The UTR #25 material is restated here so the contract is self-contained; where this report and UTR #25 differ, this report governs for SuperUnicode.

The decisive difference is the domain. UTR #25 works over the 21-bit Unicode codespace and relies on a font's MATH table for layout metrics. SUMNLS works over the full 31-bit SUCS_CP space and the 64-bit sucs_ex_char_t extended space, reserves a dedicated Native Math ExtSUCS Space for symbols Unicode cannot carry, and folds the layout metrics into the kernel itself so the renderer needs no external MATH table.

1.2 Scope

This report specifies the mathematical character repertoire and its mapping into the Bridge and the Native Math ExtSUCS Space, the Math and MathClass properties and their bitmask packing, the kernel box-model layout algorithm, and the System Control Plane math directives. It does not define a document markup language, a serialization format, or a font file format. MathML, TeX, and OpenMath remain higher-level protocols (SUTR-8 §6.3); SUF remains the font container (SUTR-4); and the property model that carries Math and MathClass is SUTR-8 (SUCPM).

1.3 Key architectural concepts

1.3.1 Mathematical alphanumeric and symbol mapping

The mathematical repertoire is mapped in two tiers. Everything the Unicode repertoire already carries is preserved as a permanent 1:1 Bridge mapping (SUTR-6): the Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols block 0x1D400–0x1D7FF, the Mathematical Operators block 0x2200–0x22FF, and the surrounding symbol blocks. Everything the repertoire does not carry — additional alphabet styles, native Greek and multi-script math alphabets, large operator assembly parts, and native fences — is allocated in the Native Math ExtSUCS Space 0x00170000–0x0017FFFF (§3).

1.3.2 O(1) property flags in SUCD

Every mathematical character carries two properties that a layout engine reads on the hot path: the binary Math property and the enumerated MathClass property, whose values mark an operator as unary, binary, relational, a fence delimiter, a big operator, punctuation, or ordinary. Both are packed into the SUCPM masks (SUTR-8 §5) so classification is a single mask test with no table walk and no heap (§4).

1.3.3 Kernel box-model and layout engine

SUMNLS defines a zero-allocation, single-pass spatial layout algorithm. The engine builds horizontal and vertical boxes for stacked fractions, radicals, extensible delimiters, and sub/superscript script tiers, computing bounding boxes and baseline offsets as it descends. It integrates directly with the SUF vector font engine, which supplies glyph bounding boxes, advance widths, and the vertical math constants; no separate MATH table is consulted (§5).

1.3.4 System Control Plane math directives

Mathematical structure that is not expressible as a character is carried in-band by a compact block of SCP markers in the 0x00110030 range: inline mathematical isolation, directional math-mode switches, alignment tab stops, and explicit grouping for fractions, radicals, and script tiers (§6).

1.4 Math specification matrix

Concern Carrier Evaluation Primary consumers
Math repertoire (Bridge) 0x1D400–0x1D7FF, 0x2200–0x22FF, symbol blocks Permanent 1:1 Bridge mapping (SUTR-6) Repertoire, charts, SUCD
Native math repertoire Native Math ExtSUCS Space 0x00170000–0x0017FFFF Native-plane range registers (SUTR-8 §4.3) Charts, native math plugin
Membership Math binary flag SUCPM core mask bit Layout engine, SUCD tooling
Classification MathClass enumerated value SUCPM extended mask field Layout engine, spacing, fences
Vertical metrics SUF glyph metrics + math constants Per-glyph register read Box-model engine (§5)
Structure and context SCP math directives 0x00110030 SCP O(1) decode (SUTR-8 §4.2) Isolation, direction, alignment

The Native Math ExtSUCS Space is a carve-out inside the Native plane (0x00120000–0x7FFFFFEF) and is currently unallocated; a native math plugin (SUTR-5) supplies its contents after the checksum gate. Until then the range contributes no characters.

2. Mathematical characters and the repertoire

2.1 The mathematical repertoire

SuperUnicode, like Unicode, includes virtually all characters used in mathematics. Following UTR #25, the repertoire is divided into three broad groups:

  • arithmetic and algebra symbols — the four operators, plus/minus, times, division, roots, factorial, and the relation set;
  • the mathematical alphanumeric symbols — styled Latin, Greek, and digit variants used as mathematical identifiers;
  • the calculus, logic, and set-theoretic symbols — n-ary operators, arrows, turnstiles, delimiters, and blackboard-bold operators.

The repertoire spans several Bridge blocks, chief among them:

Bridge block Range Role
Mathematical Operators 0x2200–0x22FF Core operators, relations, fences
Miscellaneous Mathematical Symbols-A 0x27C0–0x27EF Brackets, logical symbols
Miscellaneous Mathematical Symbols-B 0x2980–0x29FF Extended brackets and fences
Supplemental Mathematical Operators 0x2A00–0x2AFF Large n-ary and relation set
Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols 0x1D400–0x1D7FF Styled identifiers
Arabic Mathematical Alphabetic Symbols 0x1EE00–0x1EEFF Arabic math identifiers

2.2 Mathematical alphanumeric symbols and style variants

Mathematical identifiers are not styled by a font: the style is part of the character identity. A bold A, an italic A, and a script A are three distinct characters, so a formula round-trips without font context. UTR #25 formalizes the variant families; SUMNLS adopts them and extends the set in the Native Math ExtSUCS Space (§3.4).

Style Example family Bridge base
Bold bold Latin, Greek, digits 0x1D400, 0x1D6A8, 0x1D7CE
Italic italic Latin 0x1D434
Bold italic bold italic Latin, Greek 0x1D468, 0x1D71C
Script (calligraphic) script, bold script 0x1D49C, 0x1D4D0
Fraktur fraktur, bold fraktur 0x1D504, 0x1D56C
Double-struck double-struck Latin, digits 0x1D538, 0x1D7D8
Sans-serif sans, sans bold, sans italic, sans bold italic 0x1D5A0
Monospace monospace Latin, digits 0x1D670, 0x1D7F6

The base codepoints above are the first of each run; the runs are contiguous and fixed by the Bridge guarantee (SUTR-6), so a consumer addresses any variant by a constant offset from the family base.

2.3 Operators, relations, arrows, and fences

For layout, the important property is not the visual shape of an operator but its class: a relation is spaced differently from a binary operator, and a fence stretches while an ordinary symbol does not. SUMNLS therefore classifies every mathematical character with the MathClass property (§4.2) rather than by codepoint range, so a plugin-supplied native symbol is classified exactly like a Bridge symbol.

2.4 Plain-text and encoded math

A higher-level protocol may encode a formula as a linear string of math-alphanumeric characters and operators. Because the style lives in the characters and the structure is carried by SCP directives (§6), such a linear form is a complete, self-describing input to the layout engine. Markup languages (TeX, MathML, OpenMath) remain supported but are not required; they compile down to the same characters and directives.

3. Mathematical alphanumeric and symbol mapping

3.1 The Bridge mappings are permanent

The Bridge (SUTR-6) guarantees a permanent 1:1 mapping between 0x000000–0x10FFFF and Unicode. SUMNLS allocates no character inside the Bridge; it consumes the existing mappings unchanged. In particular:

  • the Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols block 0x1D400–0x1D7FF keeps its exact Unicode layout, so a style variant is addressed by its Unicode-assigned codepoint;
  • the operator and symbol blocks keep theirs;
  • no Bridge codepoint is re-purposed, renamed, or re-classified in a way that changes its identity.

This is what lets a document move between SuperUnicode and Unicode without a lossy mapping: the repertoire is shared by construction.

3.2 The Native Math ExtSUCS Space

Symbols that the Unicode repertoire cannot carry — additional alphabet styles, non-Latin math alphabets, assembly parts for extensible constructs, and native operators — are allocated in the Native Math ExtSUCS Space 0x00170000–0x0017FFFF. The range is a 16-block carve-out inside the Native plane, disjoint from the RNUR registry (0x00160000–0x0016FFFF) and from the terminal traps (0x7FFFFFF0–0x7FFFFFFF).

Block Range Contents
A — Alphanumerics 0x00170000–0x00170FFF Native styled Latin and digit variants
B — Alphabets 0x00171000–0x00171FFF Native Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic math alphabets
C — Operators 0x00172000–0x00172FFF Native n-ary, binary, and unary operators
D — Relations 0x00173000–0x00173FFF Native relations and turnstiles
E — Arrows 0x00174000–0x00174FFF Native arrow set
F — Fences 0x00175000–0x00175FFF Extensible delimiter assembly parts
G — Radicals 0x00176000–0x00176FFF Radical signs, vinculum, degree marks
H — Large operators 0x00177000–0x00177FFF Sum, product, integral, and limit forms
I — Accents 0x00178000–0x00178FFF Over/under accents and wide diacritics
J — Spacing 0x00179000–0x00179FFF Invisible operators and explicit math spaces
K — Big-op parts 0x0017A000–0x0017AFFF Assembly parts for large operators
L — Reserved 0x0017B000–0x0017EFFF Future allocation
M — Registration 0x0017F000–0x0017FFFF Plugin/registry-defined extensions

A native math symbol is allocated only through the plugin lifecycle (SUTR-5); the base standard fixes the block boundaries and leaves the contents to the native math plugin. Until the plugin is mounted the range contributes no characters, mirroring the RNUR policy in SUAS-005.

3.3 Mapping rules and invariants

  • No duplication. A symbol that exists in the Bridge MUST NOT be duplicated in the Native Math ExtSUCS Space; a native allocation is justified only when the repertoire has no Bridge codepoint.
  • Style is identity. A style variant is a distinct character, never a font selection.
  • Stable blocks. Block boundaries in §3.2 are fixed; contents within a block are assigned by the native math plugin and never renumbered.
  • Range-dispatched classification. A consumer resolves a native math character by range dispatch (SUTR-8 §4.3), not by a table of names.

3.4 Style variants as distinct characters

The variant families of §2.2 are closed for the Bridge and open for the Native space. A native plugin MAY define additional families (for example an upright italic or a bold double-struck) in Block A, provided each family is a contiguous run with a fixed base and each character carries a correct MathClass. The layout engine treats a native family exactly like a Bridge family, because it reads properties, not codepoints.

4. Math properties in SUCD and SUCPM

4.1 The Math binary property

Math is a boolean property. It is true for a character intended for mathematical use: the operator, relation, arrow, fence, alphanumeric, and delimiter sets, and false otherwise. It is the membership predicate a consumer tests before applying any math layout at all.

Math is an informative property in the SUCPM sense (SUTR-8 §1.3.1): a conformant process may use it as the default membership test, and a higher-level protocol may override it, but the layout behavior that depends on it is normative once math layout is engaged.

4.2 The MathClass enumerated property

MathClass is an enumerated property that classifies a mathematical character for spacing and layout. SUMNLS adopts the UTR #25 value set:

Value Name Atom equivalent Examples
N Normal Ord letters, digits, plain symbols
B Binary Bin plus, minus, times, union
U Unary / Prefix Op sine, log, big-operator head
R Relation Rel equals, less, subset, maps-to
O Opening Open left parenthesis, left bracket
C Closing Close right parenthesis, right bracket
F Fence Fence vertical bar, double bar, angle
P Punctuation Punct comma, semicolon (in math)
I Inner Inner a self-contained inner subformula
S Special Special prime, factorial, ellipsis

A character that is not mathematical carries no MathClass value; the property is evaluated only where Math is true. MathClass is informative, but once a consumer engages the layout engine of §5, the class determines normative spacing.

4.3 O(1) bitmask packing

Math and MathClass are packed into the SUCPM masks so classification is a single bitwise operation.

Mask Field Assigned from
sucpm_flags32_t SUCPM_F_MATH — the Math membership flag The reserved core-mask bits, by the companion SUCPM revision
sucpm_flags64_t MathClass — a 4-bit enumerated field The reserved high bits of the extended mask

SUMNLS does not itself choose the bit positions; it requires that the companion SUCPM revision assign them from the bits SUTR-8 §5 leaves reserved (bit 23 and bits 28–31 of the core mask, and the unused high bits of the extended mask), so that Math and MathClass stay reachable in O(1) from the packed mask and no existing field moves. Because the extended mask is produced by the same dual lookup engine as every other property (SUTR-8 §4), classification costs the consumer one shift-and-compare:

/* MathClass occupies a 4-bit field in the extended mask. */
typedef enum {
SUCPM_MC_N = 0, /* Normal / Ord */
SUCPM_MC_B = 1, /* Binary */
SUCPM_MC_U = 2, /* Unary / Prefix */
SUCPM_MC_R = 3, /* Relation */
SUCPM_MC_O = 4, /* Opening */
SUCPM_MC_C = 5, /* Closing */
SUCPM_MC_F = 6, /* Fence */
SUCPM_MC_P = 7, /* Punctuation */
SUCPM_MC_I = 8, /* Inner */
SUCPM_MC_S = 9 /* Special */
} sucd_math_class_t;

static inline bool sumnls_is_math(sucpm_flags64_t m) {
return (m & SUCPM_F_MATH) != 0; /* membership, O(1) */
}

static inline int sumnls_math_class(sucpm_flags64_t m) {
return (int)((m >> SUCPM_MATHCLASS_SHIFT) & 0xFu); /* class, O(1) */
}

The exact bit position of SUCPM_F_MATH and of the MathClass field is fixed by the companion SUCPM revision; the constraint SUMNLS imposes is that both are readable in O(1) from the packed mask with no allocation and no name parsing.

4.4 Vertical metrics and stretch properties

Layout needs more than a class; it needs geometry. SUMNLS derives that geometry from the SUF font engine rather than from a property table:

  • Glyph bounding box — ascent, descent, and advance, per glyph.
  • Math constants — axis height, rule thickness, gap above/below display style, superscript and subscript shifts and sizes.
  • Stretch data — the set of parts and their overlap rules for an extensible delimiter or a large operator.

These are informative at the character level and normative once the engine of §5 consumes them: a conforming renderer must produce the same box geometry given the same glyph metrics.

4.5 Derived properties

Two derived properties assist consumers that inherit math context:

  • Other_Math — true for characters that behave mathematically without being in the operator set, such as styled Greek identifiers. It is derived from the MathClass classification and the script property (SUAS-005).
  • Other_Alphabetic — true for the math-alphanumeric identifiers, so case-like processing and script resolution treat them as letters.

Both are simple closures computed by SUCD tooling (SUTR-8 §4.1); neither adds a special case to the hot path.

5. The kernel box-model and layout engine

5.1 The box model

The layout engine composes a formula from boxes. A box has a width, a height above the baseline (ascent), a depth below the baseline (descent), and an optional list of child boxes. There are two box kinds:

  • a horizontal box packs children left to right, aligned on a shared baseline, and advances by the running width;
  • a vertical box stacks children top to bottom around a central axis, used for fractions, radicals, and limits.

Boxes are allocated on a fixed, bounded stack, never on the heap. The engine's recursion depth is bounded by the nesting depth of the formula's explicit groups (§6), so a hostile input cannot exhaust memory.

5.2 Single-pass spatial layout

The engine performs one recursive-descent pass:

  1. Read the next code unit.
  2. If it is an SCP math directive, apply the structural transition (§6).
  3. Otherwise classify the character with MathClass (§4.3) and read its glyph metrics from SUF.
  4. Accumulate the glyph into the current horizontal box, applying inter-atom spacing from §5.8.
  5. When a vertical group opens, descend into a child box, lay it out, and place it relative to the parent axis.

No step allocates, and no step re-scans the input, so the pass is linear in the number of code units and O(1) per character.

5.3 Stacked fractions

A stacked fraction is a vertical box with three children: the numerator, a rule, and the denominator.

numerator
---------------- <- rule, thickness = fraction_rule_thickness
denominator

The engine:

  1. lays out the numerator and denominator as horizontal boxes;
  2. computes the rule thickness from the math constants and the current style (display, text, script, or script-script);
  3. shifts the numerator up by the numerator gap and the denominator down by the denominator gap;
  4. sets the fraction's axis height to the midpoint, so a following operator aligns to the bar.

A skewed (shilling) fraction, as in a built-up 1/2, uses the same box with a diagonal rule and a reduced numerator/denominator shift.

5.4 Radicals

A radical is a vertical box whose visible height is the height of its radicand.

_____
\/ x + 1

The engine:

  1. lays out the radicand;
  2. selects a radical sign glyph whose height covers the radicand plus the clearance above it, stretching by assembly (§5.5) when one glyph is not tall enough;
  3. draws the vinculum across the radicand width;
  4. places an optional degree at the upper-left, raised by the degree shift.

5.5 Extensible delimiters

A parenthesis, bracket, brace, vertical bar, or arrow can be built from parts. The engine selects between three strategies:

Strategy When Construction
Single glyph A glyph of the needed size exists One glyph, scaled by line metrics
Assembled Fixed end and extender parts exist Top, repeated extender, bottom
Drawn No parts exist A rule-based stroke from the glyph outline

Assembly reads the stretch data of §4.4: the available parts, their vertical coverage, and the allowed overlap. The engine repeats the extender part until the target height is met, then places the end parts. The same mechanism sizes a large operator's head (§5.7) and a radical sign (§5.4).

5.6 Script tiers

Subscripts and superscripts form script tiers. The engine maintains a current math style with four levels, following the OpenType MATH model:

Style Role Typical size
Display Whole-line formula 1.0
Text Inline formula 1.0
Script First-level sub/superscript superscript/subscript size
Script-script Second-level sub/superscript script-script size

A superscript's box is raised by the superscript shift and reduced to the next smaller size; a subscript's box is dropped by the subscript shift. A sub and a super on the same base are packed side by side with a minimum gap, and the base is followed by a prescript or postscript kernel only where the formula supplies one. Beyond script-script, further nesting stays at script-script size, matching established practice.

5.7 Big operators and limits

A big operator (n-ary summation, product, integral, union) is a character whose glyph is extended to the surrounding formula's size. Its limits are placed either as sub/superscripts or, in display style, stacked above and below the operator. The placement is chosen by an SCP directive (§6.4) or by the operator's own MathClass and the current style.

5.8 Spacing and atom classes

Between two adjacent atoms the engine inserts a space determined by their MathClass pairs, following the conventional no-space / thin-space / medium-space / thick-space table:

Left \ Right Ord Bin Rel Open Close Punct
Ord none medium thick none none none
Bin medium none none none none none
Rel thick medium none none none none
Open none none none none none none
Close none medium thick none none none
Punct thin none none none none none

A binary operator that begins or ends a formula, or that follows an opening fence, is reclassified as ordinary (unary) before spacing is applied. This rule is normative: it is what makes -x and a + -b lay out as expected.

5.9 Integration with the SUF vector font engine

SUF supplies the geometry the box model consumes:

SUF provides The engine uses it for
Glyph bounding box Box ascent, descent, advance
Math constants Axis height, rule thickness, shifts, sizes
Stretch data Extensible delimiters, radicals, big operators
Outline access The drawn-delimiter strategy (§5.5)

Because the metrics live in the font and the algorithm lives in the kernel, SUMNLS needs no external MATH table and no markup-aware shaping stage. A glyph with no outline (an invisible operator) contributes advance only.

5.10 Worked example

The linear form (a+b)/2 with an SCP fraction group lays out as:

a + b
-------
2

The engine lays out the numerator horizontal box a + b, applies binary spacing around +, lays out the denominator box 2, computes the rule from the axis height and rule thickness, shifts both by their gaps, and returns a vertical box whose baseline is the fraction axis. A following relation aligns to that axis, so the whole expression shares one baseline.

6. System Control Plane math directives

6.1 The 0x00110030 block

Mathematical structure that characters cannot express is carried in-band by a compact block of SCP markers, 0x00110030–0x0011003F. The block is disjoint from the SBR break block (0x00110020–0x00110022) and the SDF directional block (0x00110100), and it is decoded in O(1) by the SCP tier of the property engine (SUTR-8 §4.2).

ID Name Meaning
0x00110030 SCP_MATH_ISOLATE_START Begin an inline math isolation scope
0x00110031 SCP_MATH_ISOLATE_END End the innermost math isolation scope
0x00110032 SCP_MATH_MODE_LTR Switch math direction to left-to-right
0x00110033 SCP_MATH_MODE_RTL Switch math direction to right-to-left
0x00110034 SCP_MATH_ALIGN_TAB Advance to the next alignment tab stop
0x00110035 SCP_MATH_ALIGN_ROW End an alignment row and start the next
0x00110036 SCP_MATH_STYLE_PUSH Push the math style (display/text/script)
0x00110037 SCP_MATH_STYLE_POP Pop the math style
0x00110038 SCP_MATH_FRACTION_START Open a stacked fraction group
0x00110039 SCP_MATH_FRACTION_MID Separate numerator and denominator
0x0011003A SCP_MATH_FRACTION_END Close the stacked fraction group
0x0011003B SCP_MATH_RADICAL_START Open a radical group
0x0011003C SCP_MATH_RADICAL_END Close the radical group
0x0011003D SCP_MATH_LIMITS_OVER Place following limits above
0x0011003E SCP_MATH_LIMITS_UNDER Place following limits below
0x0011003F SCP_MATH_GROUP_END Close the innermost structural group

The markers are ordinary code points: they flow through SUTF (SUTR-1), SUST (SUTR-4), and SUCF canonical ordering (SUAS-004) like any other, so a formula is a plain code unit sequence.

6.2 Inline math isolation

SCP_MATH_ISOLATE_START and SCP_MATH_ISOLATE_END bracket an inline formula inside surrounding text. Isolation does three things:

  • it suspends the outer line-breaking context, so the formula is kept together unless it cannot fit (SUAS-003);
  • it establishes a math baseline independent of the surrounding text baseline;
  • it scopes the style stack, script tiers, and any directional switches, so an inner formula cannot leak state into the text around it.

Isolation is nestable; the end marker closes the innermost scope.

6.3 Directional math-mode switches

SCP_MATH_MODE_LTR and SCP_MATH_MODE_RTL select the horizontal progression order of a formula, so that an Arabic or Hebrew mathematical expression reads in its natural direction while the Latin identifiers inside it keep their own direction. The switch interacts with SUAS-001 (SDF): a formula is an isolate in the surrounding BiDi run, and the math-mode switch sets the direction of that isolate. Nested switches form nested isolates.

6.4 Alignment tab stops

SCP_MATH_ALIGN_TAB advances to the next tab stop, and SCP_MATH_ALIGN_ROW starts a new row of an aligned display (for example a multi-line derivation). Alignment is implemented as a vertical box whose rows share a set of tab-column widths; the engine measures each row, takes the maximum width per column, and re-lays the rows on the shared columns. Because the measure is over a bounded row count, the pass stays linear.

6.5 Interaction with the other standards

Standard Interaction
SUAS-001 (SDF) A math isolate is a BiDi isolate; directional switches scope within it
SUAS-002 (SGW) Math glyph advances and the monospace grid share one metric source
SUAS-003 (SBR) Isolation suppresses break opportunities inside a formula
SUAS-004 (SUCF) Math alphanumerics participate in canonical equivalence unchanged
SUAS-005 (SSP) A math alphabet resolves to its script; structure does not change script
SUTR-8 (SUCPM) Math and MathClass are read from the packed masks

6.6 Conformance of the directive block

A conformant process that renders mathematics MUST:

  • recognize the 0x00110030–0x0011003F block and apply the transition named in §6.1;
  • treat an unclosed group as closing at the end of input, without error;
  • keep the directive stream and the character stream in one code unit sequence, so no side channel is required.

A process that does not render mathematics MAY treat the block as ordinary SCP controls, which are invisible by default (SUAS-003).

7. Data files

SUMNLS adds the following machine-readable data to the SuperUnicode Character Database (SUCD), under Public/0.1.0/sucd/:

File Contents
Props/MathProps.txt The Math binary property over the Bridge and native math ranges
Props/MathClass.txt The MathClass value per mathematical character, as N, B, U, R, O, C, F, P, I, or S
Derived/MathMetrics.txt Reference math constants and per-family stretch metadata (informative)
Math/MathBlocks.txt The Native Math ExtSUCS block boundaries of §3.2

The file formats follow the SUCD conventions used elsewhere (semicolon-separated ranges, # comments). Props/MathProps.txt and Props/MathClass.txt are the authoritative inputs to the packed masks of §4.3; a bridge between them and the masks is produced by SUCD tooling, exactly as for the base properties.

8. Implementation notes

  • Freestanding C99. The engine uses a fixed-depth box stack and no heap; the depth limit is a compile-time constant.
  • One pass. The input is scanned once; a group that opens is laid out on descent and resolved on ascent, so the cost is linear in code units.
  • Properties, not tables. Classification reads the packed SUCPM mask; the engine never parses a character name or a markup tag.
  • Metrics from SUF. Bounding boxes and constants come from the font, so the same engine renders any font that supplies the required metrics.
  • Bounded stretch. Delimiter assembly is bounded by the available parts; a request beyond the font's maximum clamps to the largest construct, never loops.
  • Invisible operators. A spacing-only character contributes an advance and no ink, so explicit spacing needs no special node type.
  • Deterministic. Given the same code units and the same font metrics, the engine produces byte-identical box geometry, which makes rendering testable.

9. Recommendations

  1. Encode style in characters, not in fonts. Use the mathematical alphanumeric characters so a formula is portable across fonts and formats.
  2. Carry structure in-band. Use the SCP math directives rather than an out-of-band structure tree, so a formula is a self-describing code unit sequence.
  3. Prefer Bridge codepoints. Allocate a Native Math ExtSUCS codepoint only when the repertoire has no Bridge codepoint for the symbol.
  4. Classify by property. Never classify an operator by codepoint range; read MathClass, so native and future symbols behave identically.
  5. Keep metrics in the font. Let SUF supply geometry; do not hard-code metrics in the engine.
  6. Isolate math from text. Always bracket an inline formula with the isolation markers so it cannot disturb the surrounding line.
  7. Clamp, never fail. When a delimiter or radical cannot be stretched to the requested size, clamp to the largest available construct.

10. Stability and versioning

SUMNLS inherits the SUCPM stability guarantees (SUTR-8 §7.2) and adds the following:

  • Block boundaries are fixed. The Native Math ExtSUCS block layout of §3.2 will not be renumbered; new blocks are added only in the reserved range.
  • Directive IDs are fixed. The 0x00110030–0x0011003F assignment of §6.1 is a closed enumeration; a new structural directive requires a new block.
  • Property values may grow. The MathClass set may gain values in a future version; an existing value never changes meaning.
  • Geometry is stable per font. A font's math constants and stretch data are stable within a font version; a font update may change them and the engine follows.
  • Bridge is permanent. No Bridge math character is ever re-mapped or re-classified in a way that changes its identity (SUTR-6).

12. Terms & conventions

  • SUMNLS — SuperUnicode Mathematical Notation and Layout Support; this report (SUTR-9).
  • Math repertoire — the set of characters with the Math property true.
  • MathClass — the enumerated classification of a mathematical character as N, B, U, R, O, C, F, P, I, or S.
  • Math atom — a character, with its MathClass, considered as a unit of layout.
  • Box — a width, an ascent, a depth, and optional children; the unit of the layout engine.
  • Horizontal box — children packed left to right on a shared baseline.
  • Vertical box — children stacked around a central axis; used for fractions, radicals, and limits.
  • Script tier — a sub/superscript level at display, text, script, or script-script size.
  • Extensible delimiter — a fence grown from parts (single, assembled, or drawn) to a target height.
  • Big operator — an n-ary operator (sum, product, integral) whose glyph grows and whose limits stack.
  • Native Math ExtSUCS Space — the carve-out 0x00170000–0x0017FFFF for native math characters.
  • Math directive — an SCP marker in 0x00110030–0x0011003F.
  • Isolation — an inline math scope that suppresses outer breaking and scopes direction and style.
  • SUF — the SuperUnicode vector font engine; the source of math metrics.
  • UTR #25 — Unicode Technical Report #25, Unicode Support for Mathematics, the report this one mirrors.
  • SDF / SBR / SGW / SSP / SUCF — SUAS-001, SUAS-003, SUAS-002, SUAS-005, and SUAS-004.
